newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul economy sees some improvement but woes haunt.
newsitem.headline: Seoul economy sees some improvement but woes haunt.

text.p: The South Korean economy showed some signs of improvement on Sunday but economists were pessimistic about an imminent recovery, citing uncertain export prospects and the persistent corporate failures.
National Statistical Office (NSO) figures showed on Sunday inventories rose by 11.7 percent in May from a year earlier, the lowest growth in 20 months since September 1995.
"It's one of a few positive signs but we have still much more figures showing the economic slump will continue," said Han Sang-chun, a senior economist at the Daewoo Research Institute.
He said the lower inventory growth hardly reflected any structural improvement in the economy, which has been struggling under slowing exports amid a cyclical downturn.
An NSO report said the slowing inventory growth was made at the cost of industrial output that rose 6.1 percent year-on-year in May versus a year earlier's 10.0 percent rise.
The slower industrial output growth was attributed to production cuts by carmakers to adjust their inventory levels.
Economists said fallout from early this year's corporate failures and the subsequent debt defaults by their subcontractors were still haunting the business community.

"Instability in the financial community seriously hurt the business activities by hampering investment by companies," said Ohn Ki-un, a senior fellow at the Korea Institute for International Economics and Trade (KIET).
On Sunday the central Bank of Korea said 0.23 percent of commercial notes called in May had not been honoured, compared with 0.12 percent in May 1996 and 0.25 percent in April.
The collapses of Hanbo Steel Co in January and Sammi Steel Co in March have made lenders tighten their credit lines to companies even without major troubles.
Earlier on Sunday, two listed companies joined the string of corporate failures by announcing defaults on debt payments.
They are Tae Sung Machinery and Construction Co, an iron and steel structure manufacturer, and Keum Kang Leather Co, a leather goods maker.
Sluggish private consumption is also expected to delay a major turnaround of the economy, economists said.
In May wholesale and retail sales rose by 4.2 percent on the year, compared with a 7.6 percent growth a year ago.

"Usually it takes some time for an economic recovery to spark a pick-up in private consumption," said Ohn of KIET. "Therefore, private consumption is unlikely to gain heat until consumers become confident that the economic slump ended."
A still high unemployment level is also depressing consumption as consumers are cutting spending in response to the unstable labour market.
In May the unemployment rate stood at a seasonally-adjusted 2.6 percent, compared with 2.0 percent in the same month of 1996.
Economists said that the recent export recovery had been helped by the Japanese yen's rise and that the yen trend would remain the biggest factor for the time being.
A stronger yen would make Japanese goods more expensive, giving a comparative advantage to South Korean products that compete with Japanese goods on most export markets.

"The export recovery was made almost wholly on the back of the yen's rise rather than any improvement in other conditions," said Ohn of KIET. "It's very annoying that our exports are so heavily dependent on external factors."
The NSO figures showed ex-factory shipment for exports rose by a healthy 23.0 percent year-on-year in May, against 11.6 percent growth a year earlier and a 14.7 percent gain in April.
